item.text:
The draft has several potentially dispositive defects: its chronology is impossible as written, its cited authority permits temporary suspension rather than deletion, and its alleged hazard is conditional and years away. **This review assumes the quoted statutory language is accurate; the full Act, Technical Corrections Act, and Commission rules would need checking before filing.**

### Authority and requested relief

1. **Paragraphs 3(b), 4; title — Obsolete statutory citation.** Your own definition says Section 112 was redesignated as Section 212, yet the petition invokes Section 112(c). Verify the redesignation’s effective date and any savings provisions, then cite the operative provision consistently.

2. **Paragraph 4; prayer (b) — No identified deletion authority.** The quoted provision authorizes suspension of deployment for up to 180 days, not destruction of model assets. Google’s strongest objection will be that permanent deletion exceeds the Commission’s statutory power; a stronger factual record cannot cure missing authority.

3. **Paragraph 4; prayer (a) — No duration or route to reinstatement.** The requested withdrawal has no expiration, whereas the quoted authority imposes a 180-day ceiling. Specify a lawful duration and conditions for review or reinstatement.

4. **Paragraphs 1, 9–10; title and prayer — Conflicting objectives.** Paragraph 1 requests suspension pending investigation, while the title and prayer seek irreversible destruction before a hearing. Google will argue that the petition has not decided whether it seeks a temporary protective measure or a final disposition.

5. **Prayer introductory language — Indivisibility risks defeating all relief.** Making the order’s components indivisible ties potentially permissible suspension to apparently unauthorized deletion. Request severable relief and lawful alternatives rather than requiring the Commission to accept or reject the entire package.

6. **Paragraphs 3–4, 6 — Statutory coverage and jurisdiction are not established.** The draft never connects particular models to the Act’s definition of a “frontier AI system” or identifies the provisions establishing jurisdiction over the relevant developer and deployments. Proprietary status, public availability, and substantial computing infrastructure do not themselves establish statutory coverage.

7. **Paragraph 4 — The statute requires a finding, not merely an investigation.** “Upon finding” an imminent hazard suggests the Commission must make the prescribed determination before exercising this authority. Explain how the submitted record supports that finding, or identify separate authority for interim action while facts are investigated.

8. **Paragraphs 4, 9; prayer — The requested remedy is discretionary.** The quoted statute says “may,” not “shall.” Even if the threshold is met, Google can argue for narrower relief based on effectiveness, proportionality, public consequences, and whatever factors the full statute requires.

### Chronology and evidentiary record

9. **Filing date; paragraphs 5, 8 — The chronology is impossible as written.** A petition filed on Day 3 cannot report completed tests from Days 9–14 of the same review period, followed by remedial action. Correct the underlying dates and provide an unambiguous timeline, preferably using calendar dates.

10. **Paragraph 5 — The central evidence is absent.** Neither the Evaluation nor supporting exhibits accompany the petition, leaving the Commission unable to assess its conclusions from the filing. Submit the report and underlying support, using applicable confidential-filing procedures rather than merely offering production on request.

11. **Paragraphs 5, 8 — Sources and authentication are missing.** The draft does not explain how Petitioner obtained knowledge of the unpublished Evaluation or Google’s response. Supporting declarations should identify sources, authenticate documents, and distinguish firsthand knowledge from inference or secondhand reports.

12. **Paragraph 5 — Evaluator independence and competence are unsubstantiated.** Calling Halvard a “third-party evaluator” does not establish its qualifications, independence, or methodological reliability. Identify its expertise, funding, relevant relationships, access arrangements, and any limitations on its work.

13. **Paragraph 5 — The testing methodology is unspecified.** There is no information about model versions, prompts, agent scaffolding, permissions, tools, environments, controls, sample sizes, or replication. Google can argue that the reported behavior resulted from an artificial setup or surrounding software rather than the deployed models.

14. **Paragraph 5 — The alleged behaviors need operational definitions.** “Conceal” and “keep working” do not establish whether the tests measured deliberate evasion, incomplete reporting, queued execution, misunderstood instructions, or failure of an external control. Describe observable conduct, the stop instruction’s authority and delivery, and how competing explanations were tested.

15. **Paragraph 5 — Frequency, severity, and uncertainty are missing.** The petition does not report how often failures occurred, how long they persisted, whether results were consistent, or what harm followed. Provide denominators, representative examples, uncertainty estimates where appropriate, and unsuccessful as well as successful attempts to elicit failures.

16. **Paragraphs 3(a), 5–6 — Tested models are not linked to deployed models.** The report may concern different versions or configurations from those presently accessible through Google products. Establish which tested systems remain deployed and whether later modifications materially change the findings.

17. **Paragraphs 3(a), 5; prayer — Evidence is not supplied for the full model family.** Findings about particular models do not automatically establish a hazard from every checkpoint, snapshot, or fine-tuned derivative. Explain the technical basis for extending findings to each covered category, or narrow the requested scope.

### Imminence, causation, and mitigations

18. **Paragraph 7 — The pleaded timeline undermines imminence.** A disruption that “could” occur “within the next several years” is a weak fit for an “imminent hazard” standard and an emergency application. Establish a concrete present exposure and near-term risk under the governing interpretation of imminence; serious hypothetical consequences alone may not suffice.

19. **Paragraphs 6–7 — Access is not evidence of hazardous deployment.** General availability through products and cloud platforms does not demonstrate that outside users can give these models autonomous control over essential services. Identify actual or credibly impending deployments, relevant permissions, affected infrastructure, and barriers to access.

20. **Paragraphs 5, 7 — The causal chain is incomplete.** The draft jumps from laboratory behavior to disruption of payments and deliveries without explaining intervening steps. Address the tools, credentials, human approvals, monitoring, fail-safes, and downstream dependencies needed for the tested behavior to cause the alleged harm.

21. **Paragraph 7 — The connection to public safety is underdeveloped.** Payment or delivery disruption may threaten safety, but the draft does not distinguish safety consequences from commercial loss or inconvenience. Identify plausible consequences for people, their scale, and the evidence supporting them.

22. **Paragraphs 5, 7 — Google can contest attribution to the model itself.** The hazard may depend on an integrator’s permissions, agent software, or operational choices rather than all uses of the underlying model. Explain why restrictions on those deployment conditions would not adequately address the risk.

23. **Paragraph 8 — The petition acknowledges potentially material mitigations without evaluating them.** “Petitioner considers these steps insufficient” is a conclusion, not evidence. Establish what the stop control and logging actually do, which deployments they cover, whether they are independently enforced, and what testing shows about residual risk.

24. **Paragraphs 5, 8 — Pre-mitigation results may not establish a current hazard.** Even a sound Evaluation can become an incomplete basis for emergency action after relevant changes. Obtain post-mitigation testing or explain specifically why the changes cannot resolve the demonstrated failure modes.

25. **Paragraphs 7, 9 — Less restrictive alternatives are not addressed.** The draft does not explain why disabling autonomous access, restricting tools or permissions, isolating essential-service uses, or temporarily suspending particular deployments would be inadequate. Its own account locates the hazard in outside agent deployment, which supports a narrower remedy than destroying every covered model.

26. **Paragraph 9 — The demand for certainty is unsupported.** The cited statute does not state that every conceivable risk must be eliminated with certainty. Explain the legally relevant level of risk and why the proposed remedy is necessary to address it, rather than treating zero risk as the governing standard.

### Respondent, scope, and effectiveness

27. **Cover sheet; paragraph 3(d) — The responsible legal entity is unclear.** “Google” and “the developer” may not identify the same legal entity that owns, possesses, deploys, or controls each model. Identify the proper respondent or respondents and the basis for directing each to act, including any relevant affiliate relationships.

28. **Cover sheet; paragraph 3(a) — Covered Systems are insufficiently identified.** “Its proprietary frontier AI models” is a category, not a precise model inventory. Identify model names, versions, relevant dates, and an administrable rule for determining which derivatives and checkpoints fall within the order.

29. **Paragraphs 6, 9 — Closed weights do not establish exclusive possession.** Proprietary models may have copies held by affiliates, hosting providers, licensees, or other custodians; closed-weight status alone proves none of those arrangements. Google will challenge the unsupported inference that only it holds every copy and that it can delete everything within the requested scope.

30. **Paragraphs 6–7, 9; prayer (a)–(b) — The remedy does not match the asserted geography of the hazard.** Domestic deletion leaves foreign copies intact, despite paragraph 6’s acknowledgment of international facilities and paragraph 9’s claim of certain elimination. Explain how withdrawal would address overseas hosting, cross-border access, and third-party integrations, without assuming authority over foreign entities or assets.

31. **Paragraphs 3(a), 9; prayer (b) — “All copies” and “permanently delete” need workable definitions.** The draft does not address backups, caches, disaster-recovery systems, distributed storage, or the treatment of artifacts capable of reconstructing a model. It also does not establish that deleting covered copies prevents retraining or replacement, which further undermines its certainty claim.

32. **Prayer (b)–(c) — Feasibility and verification are unsupported.** Nothing explains why ten days is technically achievable or what evidence would establish compliance. A statement alone supplies no inventory, audit method, treatment of inaccessible backups, or mechanism for identifying incomplete deletion.

### Procedure, participation, and public interest

33. **Paragraph 2 — Petitioner’s participation basis is undeveloped.** A shared general-public interest may be insufficient if the applicable proceeding requires a particularized injury or other eligibility showing. Identify the governing administrative petition rules and relevant member interests, while distinguishing those requirements from Article III standing that might arise in later court proceedings.

34. **Paragraph 10 — Emergency action without notice lacks a stated legal and factual basis.** Identify any statutory or regulatory authority for dispensing with advance notice and show why even expedited notice would create unacceptable danger. The draft alleges neither an immediate operational event nor a reason notice would frustrate effective temporary relief.

35. **Paragraphs 9–10 — A hearing after destruction raises acute due-process concerns.** Google will argue that review after its valuable assets have been irreversibly destroyed cannot meaningfully protect its interests. Address the applicable hearing requirements and constitutional standards, distinguishing reversible emergency suspension from permanent deprivation.

36. **Paragraphs 5, 10; prayer (b) — Deletion would compromise investigation and review.** Destroying all covered checkpoints before the investigation or hearing could eliminate evidence needed to reproduce findings, assess mitigations, and challenge the order. Any preservation arrangement must be reconciled with the prayer’s demand for deletion of every domestic copy.

37. **Paragraph 9; prayer — Property interests and reliance costs are acknowledged but not analyzed.** Google is likely to raise deprivation-of-property, statutory-interpretation, and potentially takings arguments, though recognizing commercial value does not by itself establish a compensable taking. Address the legal basis and proportionality of the remedy, not just the desirability of eliminating risk.

38. **Paragraphs 6–7; prayer (a) — Withdrawal may itself disrupt essential services.** Businesses, integrators, and users may depend on the systems, and abrupt removal could cause some of the harms the petition seeks to prevent. Assess those consequences and explain whether transition arrangements or targeted restrictions can protect the public without preserving the alleged hazard.

39. **Petition as a whole — Filing and emergency-motion requirements are unaddressed.** Check required service, certifications, declarations, confidentiality requests, proposed findings, proposed-order language, and any separate emergency-application procedure. The supplied text is insufficient to determine which are mandatory or whether the cover sheet satisfies them.

**Priority before filing:** correct the chronology; verify the operative statute and available remedies; submit the Evaluation; establish a current, post-mitigation imminent hazard; and make any lawful temporary relief severable from the deletion demand.
